description:
We don't just visualize our planet. We give it a voice.

We are EarthRhythm, a team of young innovators from Peru passionate about science, technology, and creativity. Inspired by NASA's Earth Information Jukebox, we transform Earth data into interactive sounds and melodies, combining scientific exploration, accessibility, and Peruvian cultural heritage. We welcome curious minds passionate about programming, design, music, and Earth science.
summary:
EarthRhythm is an interactive educational platform that turns NASA maps of the southeastern Pacific into music. Scientific maps can be difficult to interpret, especially when the information is communicated through color alone. EarthRhythm gives learners another way to explore where the ocean was warmer or cooler than usual by pairing each map with music generated in real time.

Visitors can explore 10 interactive albums and 60 NASA map frames, meet five animated musicians, and compare how the music changes across months. Brisa provides bilingual guidance, while keyboard controls and adjustable contrast, text size, and motion let visitors choose how to explore. EarthRhythm brings together Earth science, storytelling, and sound to make NASA observations easier to understand and discuss.
details:
What does EarthRhythm do?

EarthRhythm is an interactive educational platform that turns NASA maps of the southeastern Pacific into music. Visitors can explore 10 albums and 60 NASA map frames to hear how patterns change across months. Five animated musicians accompany the experience with fictional stories inspired by real places and documented events in Peru and Colombia.

How does it work?

EarthRhythm uses stored sea surface temperature anomaly maps from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and NASA Worldview/GIBS. The browser samples each image into a grid of 28 columns and 16 rows. As the scan moves across the grid, JavaScript and Web Audio turn the color patterns into sound. Melody mode uses the patterns to shape chords and rhythms. Data mode maps the derived levels more directly to pitch. The legend shows approximate temperature differences inferred from the image colors and links to the original NASA sources.

Who is it for, and what impact do we hope to achieve?

Students, educators, and anyone who finds scientific maps difficult to read can explore the same information through images, sound, and written explanations. Brisa offers bilingual guidance, and visitors can adjust contrast, text size, and motion or navigate with a keyboard. Our goal is to give educators another way to introduce ocean science and help learners connect changes on a map with changes they can hear. Testing with learners and educators is a future step.

What did we build, and what did we consider?

EarthRhythm runs in a standard browser without an account or specialized hardware. We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, and Web Audio, with Python for the build and Node.js and Playwright for testing. Visitors can try the EarthRhythm logo or select a personal image, which is processed locally. The music is synthesized in the browser. Brisa uses OpenRouter for open-ended questions, ElevenLabs for Spanish narration, and prerecorded English guidance synthesized with Piper. Claude Design, Claude Code, and Codex assisted development. Whisper assisted transcription.
